title: IPv6: notation, link-local addresses and why migration matters

videos.script: IPv4 ran out. The last blocks were handed out in 2011, and the internet has been stretching what was left ever since. {{exhaustion}} IPv6 is the replacement, and this lesson reads it on a real network: an office that speaks both protocols at once. {{lab}} First the notation. An address is a hundred and twenty-eight bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal. Two rules shorten it, and you will expand a short one back to full length. {{notation}} Then the address every interface gives itself, starting with fe80. You will find the network card's own MAC address inside it, and see why a ping to it needs the name of an interface. {{link-local}} Then the router announcing the network's prefix, and a PC building its own global address from it, with nobody handing anything out. {{slaac}} There is no broadcast in IPv6 and no ARP. You will watch a neighbour being found without either. {{neighbours}} Last, a web server's view of the two protocols. Over IPv4 it sees the office's router. Over IPv6 it sees the PC itself. {{no-nat}} That difference is most of the reason migration matters.
